WHO World Health OrganizationThe 2012-2015 United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) is the strategic 
response of the UN Country Team in Ethiopia to national priorities articulated in the 2011-2015 
Growth and Transformation Plan. The UNDAF has been developed in close partnership with the 
Government of Ethiopia, drawing on inputs provided during consultations with development partners 
and all major stakeholders. In line with the principles of the Paris Declaration on Aid Effectiveness 
(2005) and the Accra Agenda for Action (2008), the UNDAF represents greater harmonization and 
integration of the UN system at country level, in support of Government leadership of the national 
development process.
In recent years, Ethiopia's economic performance has been remarkable, with double digit growth rates 
recorded over the past five years. A strong commitment to broad-based and pro-poor growth has seen 
Government allocate more than 60 percent of total expenditure to poverty-oriented sectors: agriculture, 
education, health, water, and road development, in recent years. Together with the support of the UN 
System and development partners, Ethiopia has thus been able to make significant strides towards 
improving key human development indicators, rating the country among the top human development 
movers worldwide, over the period 
For the coming decade, the Government of Ethiopia has in place an ambitious development plan to 
realize sustainable economic and social transformation; the goal being to achieve middle-income status 
by 2020/2023 and achieve the MDGs by 2015. This UNDAF is strategically focused on supporting 
Ethiopia's continued growth targets, the equitable distribution of the gains of growth, and the national 
transformation agenda more broadly. The country is well on track to achieve five of the MDGs, and 
looking ahead, concerted efforts will be made to scale up delivery of results and accelerate progress in 
areas where challenges remain, particularly related to improving maternal health and gender equality. 
Resources are nonetheless critical in the lead up to the 2015 historic milestone on the global development 
agenda. Sufficient resources, strategically invested in areas where there is significant potential for 
accelerated progress, may well put Ethiopia among the group of countries that would largely meet the 
MDGs, and in so doing, transform the quality of life of all Ethiopians, in particular the poorest and 
most vulnerable.
Appreciation is extended to all who contributed to the finalization of the UNDAF document, by 
providing strategic policy advice; coordinating substantive contributions; participating in consultative 
processes; and undertaking quality assurance.
We look forward to working closely together over the coming four years and beyond, to support the 
Government and the peoples of Ethiopia achieve the noble development goals that have been set.
Eugene Owusu
Resident Coordinator
of the UN System in Ethiopia

Executive Summary
The United Nations Development Assistance 
Framework for Ethiopia (UNDAF 2012–15) 
presents the planned response to the five-year national development plan for Ethiopia – the Growth and 
Transformation Plan (GTP). The GTP is the first in a series 
of three 5-year plans to propel the country’s transformation to middle income country status by 2020-2023. This 
UNDAF cycle is critical, as it coincides with the last 5 years 
of the global Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) 
campaign. It is designed, therefore, to set the framework 
for identifying innovative strategies that accelerate propoor growth and achievement of the MDGs by 2015. 
Ethiopia has registered significant progress in socio-economic development over the past decade, having maintained double digit economic growth rates, reduced poverty, improved human development indicators, and pursued 
a democratic path to ensure transparency, accountability, 
public participation, rule of law and good governance. 
Despite these results, Ethiopia remains a low-income 
country with over 20 million people living under the poverty line. The Ethiopian economy is dependent mainly on 
small-scale rain-fed agriculture, which is characterized by 
low production and productivity and is highly vulnerable 
to climate change. The contribution of the industry sector is still low and highly dominated by the informal sector. Private sector participation remains weak. Four out 
of the nine regional states of Ethiopia are lagging behind 
in almost all development indicators. Ensuring equity, 
strengthening capacities to implement policies at all levels, 
and building national resilience to climate-related, economic and other shocks remains a challenge.
The GTP’s transformation agenda seeks to double agricultural production and to re-structure the economy into 
a private sector-driven industrial economy. This will be 
supported by significant investments in infrastructure and 
an environment of inclusive democracy, public accountability, transparency and responsiveness to ensure sustainability of development efforts.
The UNDAF is fully aligned with the GTP, and aims to 
strengthen national capacities to formulate evidence-based 
policies and strategies, build strong, effective and efficient 
institutions at all levels, and improve equity in an effort 
to achieve ambitious economic and human development 
targets, including achievement of the MDGs by the target 
date of 2015. In this process, the UN will provide support to enhance participation of the vulnerable, especially 
women and children and people living with HIV/AIDS. 
Making growth sustainable and strengthening national resilience to shocks will require robust disaster risk management systems, a low carbon economic path and inclusive 
approaches to social development.
The UN will support six out of seven GTP pillars, namely: (1) 
sustaining rapid and equitable economic growth; (2) maintaining agriculture as a major source of economic growth; 
(3) creating conditions for the industry sector to play a key 
role in the economy; (4) enhancing expansion and quality 
of social development; (5) building capacity and deepending good governance; and (6) promoting gender and youth 
empowerment and equity. As a voluntary Delivering as One 
country, the UN will harmonize its contribution to these 
goals through four mutually reinforcing UNDAF pillars:
Pillar 1 Sustainable Economic Growth and Risk Reduction
Pillar 2 Basic Social Services
Pillar 3 Governance and Capacity Development
Pillar 4 Women, Youth and Children
The UNDAF addresses key cross-cutting issues which, if 
mainstreamed into the above areas, will promote responsiveness, equality, safeguarding of development gains and 
sustainability. These include: gender equity, data management, information and communication technology, HIV/
AIDS, population development, environment and climate 
change, migration and development and human rights.
The UNDAF Action Plan will build upon existing coordination and implementation mechanisms in Ethiopia, 
including those related to the Development Assistance 
Group. It also takes into account innovative and productive approaches to joint programming, drawing on 
the experience of the current eight joint programmes. 
Coherence, improved coordination and harmonization 
will be enhanced by adoption of the UNDAF Outcomes 
by all agencies as Country Programme Outcomes. 
A detailed, robust and results-based monitoring and evaluation plan will enable the UN to monitor progress towards agreed results and to address emerging challenges 
effectively. As a partner to the Government of Ethiopia, 
government generated/collected data will be a key source 
of measuring results, implying a substantial continued investment by the UN in strengthening systems to measure 
progress, enhance accountability and transparency and 
adopt mid-course corrections to reach the vision of an equitable, middle income country by 2020-2023.

Section 1: Introduction
The process of alignment and harmonization
The UN Development Assistance Framework 
(UNDAF) is a strategic planning framework 
designed jointly by the United Nations Country 
Team (UNCT) and the national host government – in 
this instance, the Ethiopian Federal Democratic Republic 
(EFDR) – to guide the UN’s contributions to implementation of the national Growth and Transformation Plan 
(GTP): Ethiopia’s current five-year development plan. 
The UNDAF 2012–15 for Ethiopia comes at a critical 
time as it undergoes a major strategic shift to embark 
on a transformational growth trajectory aimed at not 
only lifting the millions of poor people out of poverty 
but placing it strongly on the path to become a middle 
income country by 2020-2023. Ethiopia’s confidence is 
based on solid and sustained economic growth attained 
over the past decade. Ethiopia, as a voluntary UN 
‘Delivering as One’ (DaO) country, is moving ahead 
with putting in place the structures and mechanisms to 
enhance UN Reform. These efforts are central to continuous improvement in the effectiveness and efficiency 
of a coherent UN that supports national priorities. 
In the preparation of the UNDAF 2012–15, the UNCT 
in Ethiopia opted to determine its priorities based on 
the Government’s analysis, complemented by diagnostic work undertaken by the UN and other development partners. The GTP is aligned with the Millennium 
Development Goals (MDGs) timeframe and builds on 
the MDG Assessment Report of the Government of 
Ethiopia (GoE). In July 2010, GoE’s Ministry of Finance 
and Economic Development (MoFED) commissioned a 
series of situation analysis reports with a special focus on 
the needs of boys and girls. The GTP was prepared with 
extensive inputs from a wide-ranging consultation with 
civil society, the private sector, development partners as 
well as communities. This ensured that the analysis reflected the needs of the vulnerable*
. Being part of this 
process ensured the UN and donor partners contributed 
to the setting of national priorities. 
The UN Situation Analysis paper thus synthesizes and 
harmonizes findings of the GTP analysis with information from other sources. It identifies development 
challenges, constraints and opportunities. It also identifies successful approaches that have brought about 
a continued reduction in poverty and a broadening 
of the opportunity for, and access to, a more comprehensive, balanced and equitable development. In 
this regard, progress is being made to counter current 
trends towards increased regionalization and feminization of poverty and under-development.
The convergence between Ethiopia, the UN system and 
the development partners around the MDGs and the 
GTP provides the organizing principle for the UNDAF 
(2012–15). Based on its comparative advantages in relation to normative guidance, capacity development, and 
support for the provision of services, the UN prioritizes 
humanitarian and development investments with the 
aim of promoting equitable and sustainable development and rule of law. The UN’s priorities stem from 
consultation with the Government, civil society, private 
sector and donors, a review of the MDG report and other situation analyses, and a review of progress against 
the last medium-term plan, the Plan for Accelerated and 
Sustainable Development to End Poverty (PASDEP) 
2005–2010. The four strategic areas and the crosscutting issues selected by the UN for development cooperation over the period of this UNDAF are designed 
to contribute to the Government’s primary objective of 
achieving GTP targets and the MDGs. 
*  Vulnerable Groups: people who lack capacity to realize their human 
rights, have few options and few reserves and hence cannot protect 
themselves from threats, and are thus at risk of being left out of economic and social systemsUNDAF 2012-2015

The UN Country Team in Ethiopia 
The UN Country Team comprises 24 resident agencies, funds and programmes in Ethiopia, inclusive 
of specialized agencies. UN operations in Ethiopia 
cover both humanitarian and development issues, 
reflected in agency functions and mandates, which 
cover social and economic development, governance, 
human rights, technical support to capacity-building, 
social services (such as education, health, HIV/AIDS, 
water and sanitation and population) and management of natural or man-made disasters. The UN’s 
long involvement in these areas has created a large 
core of expertise and comparative advantage in research, management, building capacity and support 
to service provision. Recently, several reforms were 
introduced to improve UN coordination, effectiveness and efficiency. UN procedures are being simplified through systems like the Harmonized Approach 
to Cash Transfers (HACT), while engagement in 
joint programming builds on recognition of each UN 
agency’s added value within a diverse UN System. 
Principal reforms have included the harmonization 
of Country Programme cycles with the preparation 
of the successor UNDAF. The choice of UNDAF outcomes as country programme outcomes for various 
agencies is for example, an important milestone underlining UN commitment to Delivering as One.
UNDAF Programming principles and 
preparation processes
The UNCT in Ethiopia recognizes the importance of 
increased joint programming and programmes with 
pooling of financial and other resources to enhance 
its effectiveness and impact and to reduce transaction costs of key stakeholders. Within this framework, the UN will continue to jointly improve its 
internal systems of accountability, transparency and 
responsiveness in line with the needs of its partners. 
These efforts will be strengthened by grounding the 
UNDAF solidly on the five programming principles 
of a human rights-based approach (HRBA); gender 
equality, and the elimination of discrimination on 
the basis of sex; environmental sustainability and climate change; results-based management (RBM); and 
capacity development.
The UNDAF 2012–15 is the third*
 UNDAF prepared by the Ethiopia UNCT. The preparation process was led by GoE and responded to limitations 
and gaps in the UNDAF 2007 – 2011 by incorporating all UN assistance to Ethiopia in a focused 
framework that adhered to DAO principles. An innovative structure to manage the preparation process and enhance coordination, as well as quality of 
analysis and planning was put in place. With support 
from the Resident Coordinator’s Office (RCO), a 
Management and Planning Team (MPT) comprising 
* UNDAF 2002-2004 and UNDAF 2007- 2011 are previous frameworks.
Heads of Programmes (including Deputy Heads of 
UN Agencies), was set up. The MPT met on a weekly 
basis between June -December 2010 for the purpose 
of developing the UNDAF. The MPT was accountable to the UNCT and the Consultative Committee, 
comprising five Heads of Agencies, which provides 
overall guidance and decisions on strategic matters. 
Throughout an intense process, the RCO provided 
coordination, communication, dissemination and 
secretarial support.
Wide-ranging consultation with key stakeholders was organized in the months of September and 
October 2010 to foster ownership. A well attended 
prioritization workshop organized jointly by the UN 
and GoE – in which civil society, private sector and 
donors participated – helped the UN identify key 
priority themes. Aligned to the GoE’s priorities as 
enunciated in the GTP, these themes also furthered 
UN mandates on good governance, social protection, and humanitarian assistance within an overall 
commitment to human rights based programming. 
Thematic Working Groups (TWGs) were organized 
around these priority themes and tasked with designing the strategy and outcome statements, taking into 
account agencies’ mandates, capacities and comparative advantage in relation to other development partners. Representatives from relevant GoE ministries 
were members of TWGs, ensuring that strategies and 
agreed outcomes were based on national strategies 
and priorities. Photo Credit – UNFPA6
SECTION 2: DEVELOPMENT CONTEXT 
Country background
Ethiopia is a federal state with nine regional 
states and two city administrations. In 1991, 
under the leadership of the Ethiopian People’s 
Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), Ethiopia 
embarked on an ambitious transition from a centralized undemocratic government to a democratic state. 
The country has since then held four elections and 
established a decentralized system of governance. 
Bordered by Eritrea, Djibouti, Kenya, Somalia and 
Sudan, Ethiopia is located within a fragile geo-political context and by the end of 2010 was the host 
to 145,000 refugees from neighbouring countries. 
Instability in neighbouring countries - notably in 
Sudan, which has undergone a referendum for secession of the south of the country; and Somalia, which 
continues to be plagued by factional fighting - makes 
Ethiopia more vulnerable to regionally induced 
shocks that may affect development efforts. 
With a population of 79.4 million, Ethiopia is the 
second most populous country in sub-Saharan 
Africa (SSA), with 83 per cent of people living 
in rural areas. Women still lag behind their male 
counterparts on many key human developement
indicators, resulting in a ranking of 121 among 134 
countries in relation to the gender gap.* Ethiopia’s 
economy is highly dependent upon rain-fed and 
mainly subsistence agriculture, which constitutes 
41 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), with 
services now the leading economic sector at 46 per 
cent of GDP and industry at 13 per cent. 
With a vision to become a middle income country, 
Ethiopia has implemented national programmes to 
accelerate economic growth, with poverty reduc-

tion as a central policy concern. The Sustainable 
Development and Poverty Reduction Programme 
(2002/03–2004/05) focused on improving human 
and rural development, food security, and capacity 
building through transformation of the agricultural 
sector; reforms in both the justice system and the 
civil service; decentralization and empowerment; 
and capacity building in the public and private sectors. This was followed by the PASDEP, an MDGbased plan that took bold steps towards accelerated 
growth with an emphasis on commercialization of 
agriculture; private sector development; and scaling up of investments in pro-poor interventions to 
achieve the MDGs. This was accompanied by an increase in the share of total expenditure directed at 
spending on poverty-targeted sectors from 42 per 
cent in 2002/03 to over 64 per cent by the end of 
2007/08. 
The Government of Ethiopia designed a new fiveyear plan (GTP) for 2010/11–2014/15. The GTP 
aims to foster broad based development in a sustainable manner to achieve the MDGs. The plan envisages a major transformation of the national economic 
structure, seeking to double agricultural production 
and significantly increase the share of industry in the 
economy. It emphasizes investment in economic and 
social infrastructure, while maintaining a focus on 
human development, women’s empowerment and 
governance. The plan sets ambitious targets, including: to achieve 75 per cent access to electricity and 
total access to safe water by 2015, to reduce the infant mortality ratio from 101 to 68 (per 1,000 live 
births) and cut the maternal mortality ratio (MMR) 
by more than half from 590 to 267 (per 100,000 live 
births). The GTP is the anchor on which the United 
Nations Development Assistance Framework (2012–
15) is based.7
Economic growth and poverty
Ethiopia has sustained a double-digit growth rate of 
11 per cent over the past five years with improvements in food security and human development indicators and declining poverty.
Growth has been largely broad-based. The three 
main sectors (agriculture, industry and services) are 
all growing at a healthy 8 per cent or more per annum with an increasing proportion of benefits accruing to the 83 per cent of the Ethiopian population living in rural areas. However, with an annual 
population growth rate of 2.6 per cent, the Ethiopian 
Government has recognized the need to address population issues in order to promote sustainable development. Tax revenue has declined relative to GDP 
and exhibited a shift in structure with a modest decline in direct tax and growing reliance on foreign 
trade tax at federal level. The declining tax revenue 
relative to GDP is a source of concern, compromising 
GoE’s ability to spend on pro-poor growth.
Ethiopia’s key growth strategy is Agricultural 
Development Led Industrialization (ADLI), recognizing the importance of agriculture as the dominant 
source of the nation’s income. The rural population 
remains largely dependent on rain-fed subsistence 
agriculture, animal husbandry or wage labour for its 
livelihood. However, the agricultural sector is characterised by low production and productivity, degradation of land, poor water management, and low levels 
of technology usage. Pre- and post-harvest losses, currently estimated between 30 - 40 per cent (Dejene, 
2006) and the underdeveloped marketing system further undermine incentives to increase productivity.
Female farmers’ access to resources including land 
and extension services is limited. Women constitute 
19 per cent of agricultural land owners in Ethiopia, 
while men constitute 81 per cent (Central Statistical 
Agency (CSA), 2007/08). Furthermore, female farmers’ lack of diversified assets impacts their capacity to 
respond successfully to environmental and economic 
shocks. An estimated 50 per cent of land resources 
are degraded and 85-90 per cent of Ethiopian agriculture is rain-fed. As of 2009/10, the total irrigable 
land developed by irrigation (GTP) is 2.5 per cent. 
Current rainfall patterns coupled with rapid population growth and consequent land degradation threaten to further reduce the productivity of agriculture 
and increase vulnerability to drought, which can 
significantly reduce agricultural production if not 
addressed. Therefore, despite growth in agricultural 
production, food security remains very challenging 
both at national and household levels.*
Despite possessing one of the largest livestock populations in Africa and livestock accounting to about 30-
40% of the country’s Agricultural GDP and contributing 
significantly to the livelihood of an estimated 80 % of 
the rural population productivity of Ethiopian livestock 
remains abysmally low. Meat production for example is 
estimated to be about 8.5 kg./cattle/year which Is significantly lower than in Kenya and Senegal (21 and 16 kg. 
respectively).Per capita consumption of milk and dairy 
products is just 22 kg of milk equivalent in Ethiopia , far 
below than that of Sudan( 160kg.) and Kenya( 80 kg.)
Agriculture is also currently the main source of 
Ethiopia’s foreign exchange earnings. Export performance has been evaluated monthly by the Ministry 
of Trade and subsequently by the National Export 
Steering Committee. Ethiopia’s exports have diversified and increased, with 86 per cent of the revenue target of USD 1,727.5 million met in 2007/08 (PASDEP 
Annual Review, 2009). Coffee accounted for 35.5 per 
cent, and oilseeds, pulses, cut flowers, khat, leather 
and leather products accounted for 46.1 per cent. 
DAC data show that the proportion of imports from 
Ethiopia to that of total imports from developing and 
least developed countries (LDCs) admitted free of 
duty, for all product categories, has been consistently 
larger than the SSA and LDC average.
The basic assumption of ADLI is that industrialization and urbanization would be derivative processes 
flowing naturally from a rapid growth of the agricultural sector. The GTP recognizes that strategic investments are required to diversify and transform the 
economy. Industry has a series of very ambitious targets, to be achieved during the GTP period to address 
the current serious shortages of supply and factor inputs, which are necessary for accelerated growth.
Mining efforts by the Ministry of Mines and Energy 
have intensified with increasing numbers of licenses 
awarded to foreign and domestic companies interested in exploration, mining and petroleum exploration and development, combined with expanding the

decentralization has taken place with the formation 
of artisanal mining associations. The sector already 
generates foreign capital with USD 99.5 million secured from exports in 2007/08 and internal revenue 
of over 500 million birr in the same year. Telecom 
subscriptions have increased but overall penetration 
remains low with an average of three mobile phones 
per 200 people. The Rural Connectivity Programme 
plans to lay a further 6,000 kilometres of optic fibre 
to increase electricity coverage to 41 per cent (GTP). 
The national MDG-linked road target was exceeded 
with 49,000 kilometres of roads constructed (GTP).
Growth is expected from an expanded privatization 
programme, support for job creation through micro 
and small-scale enterprises and increasing bilateral 
and multilateral trade linkages. The latter has focused on accession to the World Trade Organization. 
Currently, unemployment nationally remains at 14 
per cent. Women’s employment in industries is lower 
than for men; the rate of female employment is at 
a mere 27.9 per cent, and women on average earn 
about 86 per cent of what men earn. On the other 
hand, women comprise more than 60 per cent of 
those engaged in the informal sector.
Gender gaps in terms of access to micro-credit and 
financial services, inadequate entrepreneurship and 
managerial capacity, and skills to successfully set up, 
run and expand businesses, are significant constraints 
to women’s economic empowerment and equality.
The growing rural–urban migration is contributing 
to rising urban unemployment, which in turn has led 
to increased international migration. Environmental 
degradation with growing economically active populations has also increased labour and forced migration both within the country and across its borders. 
With an estimated 50 per cent of the population below the age of 20 years, Ethiopia increasingly faces 
high youth unemployment and under-employment 
both in the rural and urban areas. Though it is difficult to accurately estimate the magnitude of irregular 
migration, there are some assessments and research 
that show the huge increase in migration within and 
from Ethiopia, in particular by young people.
Increased investment in the education and health 
sectors has resulted in improved human development 
indicators. Poverty levels have reduced from 38.7 per 
cent in 2004/05 to 32.7 per cent in 2008/09 and to 
an estimated 29.2 per cent in 2010 (MoFED, 2010a). 
Between 2000 and 2010, the human development index (HDI) for Ethiopia improved by an annual average growth rate of 2.73 per cent, from 0.250 to 0.328 
– making it the third fastest growth rate in the world 
since 2000. Even so, Ethiopia’s HDI still ranks 157 
out of 169 countries (UNDP, 2010). 
The Ethiopia MDG Report of 2010 suggests the 
country is likely to achieve most MDG goals by 2015 
with the exception of MDG 3 and MDG 5 (MoFED, 
2010a). There are significant improvements in primary school enrolment (from 33 per cent in 1992 to 
a current 95.9 per cent (93 per cent for female and 
98.9 per cent male); a steady decrease in under-five 
mortality per 1,000 live births from 140 in 2000 to 
101 in 2009/10 (GTP); a decline in MMR from 873 in 
2000/01 to 590 in 2009/10 (GTP). Access to clean water also increased from 47.3 per cent of the population 
in 2005/06 to 68.5 per cent (GTP). The GTP seeks to 
achieve 75 per cent in electricity coverage; and 98.5 
per cent in potable water coverage by 2015.
Despite these impressive achievements, Ethiopia remains a least developed country with significant challenges. Improvements in life expectancy, which can be 
seen as a good proxy indicator of the overall develop- UN Photo/Eskinder Debebe9
mental gains, are rather modest. Furthermore, while 
poverty in urban areas is slightly less than in rural areas, urban poverty is decreasing at a slower rate and 
inequity is increasing at a higher rate than in rural 
Ethiopia. Despite a decline in the overall proportion 
of the poor, with population growth there is an increase in the absolute number of poor people. Poverty 
continues to have a strong regional bias; while gains in 
reducing poverty have not yet translated to significant 
reductions in hunger or acute malnutrition. 
The various effects of climate change will have a 
negative impact on economic growth rates and adversely affect prospects for achieving GTP and MDG 
targets. Agriculture, water, energy, infrastructure, 
health and biodiversity will be the primary sectors 
affected by climate change. Limitations in capacity, 
finance and technology at all levels hinders climate 
change adaptation and response measures. The GoE 
has committed itself to building a low-carbon and 
climate resilient economy by 2025. The Government 
has also established more than 80 Nationally 
Appropriate Mitigation Actions (NAMA) that are 
mostly linked to renewable energy.
Recognizing the need for strengthening the National 
Statistical System to improve the monitoring and 
evaluation (M&E) of development outcomes, the 
GoE has been progressively allocating significant resources for various socio-economic and demographic 
sample surveys and censuses. 
The GTP identifies Information and Communication 
Technology (ICT) development as an essential component in achieving objectives in all sectors. The 
scope of ICT in the GTP context is broad, outlining development of: systems; regulatory policies; 
standards and standardization; information services; 
infrastructure; education, training and learning; and 
ICT culture. ICT is, and can be, an enabler in nearly 
all aspects of government, service provision, administration, communication and information dissemination. The opportunity for adoption of ICT in the 
development environment will increase across the 
board as basic infrastructure continues to improve 
and relative prices continue to fall

Governance and participation
In line with the GoE’s long-term vision of becoming a middle-income country where democracy 
and good governance are maintained through 
people’s participation and where good will and 
social justice are secured, the GTP identifies good 
governance, human rights and capacity building 
as one of its strategic pillars. It underscores the 
importance of making progress in these areas as 
an important pre-requisite for attainment of its 
development objectives.
Ethiopia has comprehensively incorporated human 
right principles in its Constitution. Chapter three of the 
Constitution provides an extensive list of civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights. International 
human rights standards and instruments, including 
the Universal Declaration on Human Rights, are also 
cited within the Constitution. Ethiopia is a party to 
seven of the eight core international human rights instruments, has signed but not ratified the Optional 
Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the 
Child (CRC) concerning the involvement of children 
in armed conflict, but has yet to sign or ratify any of 
the other optional protocols to international human 
rights treaties (primarily concerning mechanisms for 
individual complaints). Ethiopia has also ratified the 
AU’s African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the 
Child, and has signed but not yet ratified the Protocol 
to the African Charter on Human and People’s Rights 
on the Rights of Women in Africa.
Human rights have also been given due prominence in 
the fight against poverty where the PASDEP reaffirms the 
GoE’s commitment “to open, transparent, and democratic governance that respects the rights of all of its citizens, as enshrined in the Constitution” (MoFED, 2006). 
This is in line with global consensus that poverty is not 
only a matter of income but more fundamentally an interconnected web of mutually reinforcing deprivations.
The GoE has, through commendable effort, recently 
submitted all its outstanding reports to the UN human 
rights treaty bodies, the African Commission on Human 
and Peoples Rights (ACHPR) (apart from its state report 
on the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of 
the Child, due in 2004) and the Human Rights Council 
with the support of the Ethiopian Human Rights 
Commission (EHRC) and the UN. Ethiopia also underwent the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) in December 
2009, and committed to implement most of the UPR 
recommendations on human rights.
Progress has been recorded in many areas: strengthened institutional capacity in the EHRC can be measured from support the Commission provided to GoE 
that enabled outstanding reports to international human rights mechanisms to be cleared. In addition, 
community outreach and public awareness-raising 
on human rights, the monitoring of human rights, 
increased integration of human rights in higher education institutions and the preparation of the first 
National Human Rights Action Plan and first human 
rights situation report are other indicators of strengthened capacity. Some challenges persist, however, that 
require continued attention. These include support 
to strengthening the capacity of national human 
rights institutions in the promotion and protection of 
human rights; strengthening national capacities for 
mainstreaming human rights in all aspects of policy, 
legislation, implementation and M&E; strengthening 
the culture of human rights; increasing the focus on 
economic, social and cultural rights; adequately integrating human rights into the work of public institutions; increasing the harmonization of national laws 
with the constitutional bill of rights and international 
instruments; and building the coverage and capacity 
of civil society organizations (CSOs) to complement 
the work of the EHRC at grassroots level.

Progress against MDGs
Summarizing Ethiopia’s overall progress 
towards the MDGs
Ethiopia has demonstrated impressive development 
gains over the last five years. The economic growth 
of the last decade and progress towards the MDGs 
has been significant. The economy had an average 
annual growth rate of 11 per cent, well above the 
7 per cent estimate required to achieve the goal 
of poverty reduction (MDG 1) by the year 2015. 
Government also made progress in the provision of 
social services such as education, health and infrastructure by spending a large share of its budget in 
these pro-poor sectors. Expenditure on social protection measures has however, been on the decline. 
Presuming continued support from the international 
community to address challenges noted in this document, the country is on a positive and promising 
track toward meeting most MDGs, either wholly or 
partially.

MDG 1: Eradicating extreme poverty 
and hunger
Economic growth has emanated from the sustained 
growth of smallholder private agriculture, resulting in 
significant reductions of poverty, particularly in rural 
areas. This is despite low levels of productivity and 
limited utilization of water resources for agriculture. 
Even though the agricultural sector continued to be 
the major driver of the economy, the growth contribution of the non-agricultural sectors (particularly 
service sector) has also been significant. The agricultural and service sectors together have contributed 
the lion’s share to GDP. During the last seven years, 
agriculture (including allied activities) and service sectors have contributed 41 per cent and 46 per cent on 
average to total GDP, respectively. Moreover, this 
expansion has also been broad based with significant 
contribution from manufacturing, and construction 
sectors. Overall poverty in Ethiopia is on the decline 
and is estimated at 29.2 per cent in 2009/10. Income 
poverty during 2004/05 is slightly higher in rural

especially for non-registered dwellers in urban areas 
(WFP/UNICEF, 2009). Poverty and food insecurity 
have a strong gender bias, as female-headed households continue to be disproportionately affected.*

MDG 1 is high. However, Ethiopia’s high vulnerability 
to disaster risks may adversely impact poverty reduction 
and food security investments if risks are not adequately managed. In addition, achieving further reductions 
in malnutrition continues to be a challenge. Although

Concerted efforts are being made to contain the

2010, the total number of PLHIV currently on

of those in need at that time.** This total included

According to the Ministry of Health (MoH), in 
2005/06, malaria was the leading cause of death in 
the country. The household level insecticide treated 
net (ITN) coverage rate in malaria-prone areas increased to 100 per cent in 2009/10. Facility-based 
data illustrates that morbidity due to malaria declined by 48 per cent, hospital admissions by 54 per 
cent and mortality by 55 per cent. The case fatality 
rate for malaria in age group five years and older, fell 
to 3.3 per cent and in under-five year olds to 4.5 per 
cent (target 2 per cent for both). Although a majority 
of women (74.6–79 per cent) reported having heard 
about malaria, only 38.2 per cent in susceptible areas

Areas that require further efforts include increasing 
indoor residual spraying coverage, improving DDT 
resistance, and the utilization of ITNs. The treating 
of persons who test negative, and better adherence 
to rapid diagnostic tests for the treatment of fever 
caused by pneumonia, will also go a long way toward the realization of this goal. It is imperative to 
work on the further integration of malaria within the 
Health Extension Programme (HEP) and ensure continued advocacy for funding and increased surveillance.
Ethiopia ranks 7th among the top twenty-two 
Tuberculosis (TB) High Burden Countries in the 
world, and one of the top three in Africa, with regard 
to the estimated number of cases of tuberculosis. The 
incidence rate of all forms of TB is estimated at 378 
per 100,000 in 2009/10, while the incidence rate of 
smear-positive TB is 163 per 100,000.
The tuberculosis (TB) death rate per 100,000 people 
has slightly declined from 94 in 2004 to 92 in 2007, 
partly as a result of adopting the direct observed 
treatment short course (DOTS) strategy as well as 
prevention and control interventions integrated in 
the HEP.*** As a result, in 2009, 92 per cent of all 
public health centres and hospitals were providing

is good, at 84 per cent in 2008/09, but the case detection rate is stagnant at 34 per cent (MoFED/UN, 
2010). TB indicators were quite stable in 2009/2010

rate of 35.8 per cent; TB treatment success rate at

MDG 7: Environmental sustainability
Ethiopia is known as one of the world’s biodiversity hotspots (MoA, 2010). The wide range in elevation creates extreme spatial variations of climate 
that has led to a variety of ecosystems, which host 
numerous plant and animal species, many of which 
are endemic to the country. There are 12 major river 
basins discharging an estimated annual flow of 122 
billion cubic metres. All of the major rivers are international and thus provide vital freshwater to neighbouring countries. Ethiopia is often described as the 
“water tower” of north-eastern Africa. However, the 
variations in elevation and climate across the country create an uneven distribution of available water 
resources. Average annual rainfall varies from less 
than 200 millimetres in the lowlands to over 2,200 
millimetres in parts of the highlands. Rainfall is also 
intense. Over 75 per cent of the total surface runoff occurs in four months of the wet season (June to 
September) (MoA, 2010).
Large-scale land degradation in Ethiopia resulting 
from population pressure, overgrazing, soil erosion, 
encroachment on bush and rangelands, deforestation, and unsustainable land management practices 
poses a huge challenge to sustainable improvements 
in food security and agricultural productivity enhancement. Estimates of original forest cover and 
deforestation rates differ from one source to another, but the general consensus is that the scale 
of clearance has been massive and the remaining 
forest terrain is being depleted at an alarming rate 
(Million, 2010). 
Policy measures such as the late 2005 Biodiversity 
Strategy and Action Plan indicate that Ethiopia has 
a commitment to integrating the principles of sustainable development into its development planning. 
However, efforts to protect biodiversity have not 
shown similar progress: the proportion of terrestrial 
areas protected to total surface area grew by a mere 
one-third of a percentage point in the period 1990–
2008 (MoFED, 2010a). Nevertheless, in 2006 a sustainable land management platform was established 
and by 2010 an associated multi-stakeholder strategic investment framework was launched. Also, a 
campaign initiated during the Ethiopian Millennium

MDG 8: Global partnership for development
Although Ethiopia is making great progress in increasing domestic revenue, a substantial amount of Ethiopia’s 
national budget is financed from external sources. 
According to a 2007 Development Assistance Group 
(DAG) report, Ethiopia’s official development assistance 
(ODA) per capita is still significantly lower than the SSA 
average. A significant portion of this external assistance 
is humanitarian aid (30–50 per cent of total aid). The 
report stresses the need for scaling up external financing 
and aid to help Ethiopia reach the MDGs. 
A large portion of total ODA finances emergency 
food assistance and social infrastructure services 
like education, health, water supply and sanitation, 
population control and reproductive health. Donor 
commitment is needed in the productive sectors, as 
illustrated by the low volume of ODA in agriculture, 
industry, trade policies and regulations. There is also 
need to improve the quality of aid – in particular, its 
predictability and effectiveness. The aid dependency 
ratio of Ethiopia as measured relative to gross national income is high, especially when compared to 
SSA and low income economies. More than 50 per 
cent of the gross capital formation of the country is 
financed by aid. This is 2.3 times the SSA average 
and more than double of low income economies. 
Ethiopia has a mature aid coordination mechanism 
in the DAG, with a secretariat and senior staff support that, in line with the Paris Declaration and harmonization principles, works to promote donor-government coordination and aid effectiveness.
The formal and informal flow of remittances to 
Ethiopia has increased considerably and is estimated 
to be over a billion dollars in recent years. This trend 
not only supports the country’s balance of payments 
but has also directly improved the lives of a substantial number of families and individuals. Still, a large 
proportion of remittance flows is informal and mainly used for personal consumption; hence the need 
to improve the flow of remittances through formal 
channels to broaden investment options.

The UN will coordinate its work through the UN 
Governance TWG, and harmonize through engagement with the DAG Governance TWG and other existing coordination mechanisms.
Pillar 4: Women, Youth and Children
Women, youth and children constitute a significant 
proportion of the total Ethiopian population and are 
experiencing multifaceted political and socio-economic challenges. Recognizing this, the government has 
been undertaking significant efforts to address these 
concerns with some encouraging developments and 
results in sectors such as education and health. The 
Ethiopian Constitution lays the foundation for the 
advancement of gender equality and women’s rights. 
More recently, the GTP and the Sector Development 
Plan for Women and Children included the following issues among their policy priorities: women’s 
economic empowerment; participation of women in 
political and decision-making processes; improvement of women’s health status; protection of women 
and girls from discriminatory attitudes; harmful traditional practices and violence; and improvement of 
quality of life for women and girls through their active engagement and participation in environmental 
protection and management. 
However, much more is required to ensure that 
women, youth and children actively participate in, 
and benefit from, the development process. The recently restructured Ministry of Women, Children 
and Youth Affairs (MoWCYA) is well positioned to 
address the interconnected and interrelated concerns 
of women, youth and children in a coordinated and 
holistic manner. Hence, the women, youth and children pillar of UNDAF attempts to support ongoing 
government-led national efforts in this regard.
The UNDAF pillar on women, youth and children delivers its support under two outcomes, as outlined below. 
UNDAF Outcome 12: By 2015, women and 
youth are increasingly participating in advocacy, social mobilization and decision making 
and benefiting from livelihood opportunities 
and targeted social services.
The UN will provide important financial and technical support to enhance the level of participation of 
women and youth in decision-making processes at 
different levels and to increase their livelihood opportunities. At the same time, targeted efforts will 
aim to improve access and utilization of critical social services designed to improve the health, education and wellbeing of women and youth. 
The UN will work to strengthen the capacity of institutions providing financial and non-financial services 
to support economic empowerment of women and 
youth. It will also support – through specific programmatic interventions – the provision of accessible 
and affordable financial services to aspiring women 
entrepreneurs, including enhancing the competitiveness and profitability of female-owned businesses.
To help create an environment that empowers women to reach their optimal potential in all areas of life, 
women need education and skills that are marketable in the workplace and make them increasingly 
employable. This needs to be accompanied by social 
transformation regarding negative gender stereotypes and behaviours so they are able to take part in 
decision-making and policy planning processes that 
directly impact the quality of their lives. 
UN support to strengthen women’s participation in 
decision-making will be targeted towards: increasing 
women’s representation in legislative organs, the judiciary and decision-making positions in the government, non-governmental and private sectors; building 
capacity in leadership skills; and strengthening women’s associations and other types of organizations.

Youth, especially those out of school and in disadvantaged situations, need additional strategies and 
programmatic responses to enable them to compete for, and benefit from, livelihood opportunities. 
Young women especially need to be equipped with 
knowledge, skills and capacity to make informed decisions regarding their reproductive health, including 
protecting themselves from HIV and other sexually 
transmitted infections.
The UN will support policy and strategy development, focusing on: the implementation of the 
National Youth Act which is currently awaiting ministerial endorsement; and the implementation of the 
Youth Development Package. Continued efforts will 
build capacity for the utilization of normative guidelines, manuals and standards on youth voluntarism, 
life skills, youth-centre functional standards, economic strengthening activities and participation.
Youth empowerment and participation emphasize 
comprehensive programmes that focus on multipronged and balanced adolescent development, encompassing of social, physical and emotional aspects. 
Youth-adult partnerships that work to improve gender equity, improve girls’ participation, and enhance 
child protection will be enhanced through youth dialogue, life skills/peer education, media development, 
youth leadership, and girls’ empowerment through 
Assertive Action training. Service delivery will focus 
on youth centres, youth friendly sexual and reproductive health services, playgrounds, recreational 
centres, youth friendly health services, VCT services 
and condom promotion.
UNDAF Outcome 13: By 2015, women, youth 
and children are increasingly protected and rehabilitated from abuse, violence, exploitation 
and discrimination.
In this UNDAF, priority is given to initiatives that 
will enable women and young people to demand 
their rights while supporting the establishment or 
further development of mechanisms that will protect 
women, youth and children from abuse, violence, exploitation and discrimination. 
The first focus area is on social mobilization to address the underlying root causes of the problems of 
violence and discrimination by actively engaging 
individual citizens and communities as claim holders in a policy dialogue process and by supporting 
advocacy on the rights of women and children. The 
second focus area deals with institutional capacity 
building of law enforcement and other relevant bodies (as duty bearers) with the aim to support effective implementation and reinforcement of relevant 
policy and legal frameworks. Specific emphasis will 
be given to raising awareness of law enforcement 
agencies, including the police and the judiciary, on 
legal frameworks that deal with distinct women’s 
and children’s rights, such as the Family Law and 
the Penal Code. Furthermore, this specific UNDAF 
outcome will seek to support enhanced provision of 
appropriate rehabilitation services for survivors of 
violence and abuse. 
The development and effective implementation of a 
national GBV strategy will contribute to the development of a coordinated approach that will bring 
together different policy components for addressing 
GBV, such as psychosocial support, legal aid, and social reintegration for survivors. 
Addressing risk reduction and protective interventions is critical in determining the future wellbeing 
of adolescents, especially for young adolescent girls. 
GBV and early marriage are of major concern for 
adolescent girls, equally vulnerable to HIV infection 
and early pregnancy, as well as physical and emotional threats and risks to their rights in the areas 
of education and employment. In addition, improved 
measures of support and cooperation are required 
with key social institutions and protection networks 
that decrease vulnerability and risk-taking behaviours. 
Child protection strategic investments relate to: children being safe from violence and abuse; children 
being protected from exploitation; children having 
a minimum standard of care and support; and children having access to justice. In addition, the social

Strategies will include the promotion of child protection systems and social change, with an emphasis

Cross-cutting issues
The UN supports and implements a gender mainstreaming approach to strengthen the gender dimension of other UNDAF thematic priorities and pillars. 
More specifically, priority will be given to strengthening the institutional capacity of sector Ministries, 
notably MoWCYA, MoFED and CSA, in gender 
mainstreaming, gender-responsive budgeting and 
gender-responsive monitoring. These initiatives will 
be complemented by UN support for the systematic 
collection and gender analysis of sex-disaggregated 
data to feed into policy making, planning and monitoring across sectors. Strengthening accountability 
systems, improving the use of performance assessment tools to regularly monitor the results and effectiveness of gender mainstreaming, and contributing 
to increased coordination among sectors and among 
women’s structures at federal, regional and woreda levels on gender issues, will also feature among 
UNDAF priorities. 
Cross-cutting concerns related to population issues, 
HIV/AIDS, and environmental protection will be directly addressed in the design of UN support, from 
the perspective of women and youth as agents of 
change within the broader community. In addition, 
interventions promoting the increased access to services by women and youth; as well as their engagement in decision-making processes that affect their 
well-being - will be supported. 
Partnerships and coordination
The UN system has a strong mandate, experience and 
strategic tools to address challenges related to gender 
equality, women’s empowerment, youth participation 
and child protection. The UN system provides normative guidance and strategic advice on policy development that enables the country to meet its obligations 
under the Convention on the Elimination of all forms 
of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) and the 
Convention of the Rights of the Child (CRC). 
The UN will continue to work closely with the 
Gender Sector Working Group and the Donor Group 
on Gender Equality to ensure an effective and coordinated policy response to the challenges associated 
with gender equality and women’s empowerment in 
Ethiopia.

Section 5: Implementation arrangements
UNDAF Governance and Implementation Structure
S
ince 2010, Ethiopia is formally considered a 
voluntary Delivering as One (DaO) country. 
The recognition of Ethiopia as a voluntary DaO 
country is an important step to further strengthening 
the lead role of GoE in the UN Reform process and 
to consolidating the commitment of the UN to move 
forward towards increased system-wide coherence.
The UN and the GoE have jointly adopted an incremental approach to roll out DaO reform in the country, with the UNDAF being the driver for enhanced 
UN programme coordination and system-wide coherence. Through the UNDAF, the UN in Ethiopia 
aims to achieve greater effectiveness and efficiency by 
reflecting a unified UN response to national priorities 
identified in the Growth and Transformation Plan. 
Efforts to deepen harmonization through joint programming and joint programmes will be intensified.
The governance structure tasked with overseeing the 
development of an UNDAF Action Plan, and implementation thereafter, will be as follows:
High level steering committee (HLSC)
A high level steering committee composed of the 
Government, the UN and development partners provides high-level direction and oversight to the implementation of the UNDAF and the DaO reform in 
Ethiopia. The committee will annually review progress against the UNDAF Results Matrix and approve 
the preparation of new joint programmes to implement UNDAF. 
United Nations Country Team (UNCT)
The UNCT is composed of representatives of the 
UN funds and programmes; specialised agencies and 
other UN entities accredited to Ethiopia. The UNCT, 
under the leadership of the Resident Coordinator, 
will work to achieve demonstrable results and ensure 
the delivery of measurable results in support of the 
development agenda of the Government. 
The UNCT oversees the development and implementation of UNDAF and the work of the Technical 
Working Groups (TWGs); the Communication 
Group and the Operations Management Team.
Inter-agency programme team (IAPT)
An inter-agency programme team, comprising Heads 
of Programmes from all UN Agencies, and/or Deputy 
Heads of Office, will be established to provide strategic leadership at the technical level in the formulation of an UNDAF Action Plan and in subsequent 
implementation. Working through TWGs will ensure the timely completion and quality achievement 
of UNDAF results through a participatory process 
that involves as many UN colleagues across various 
UN agencies.
Joint programming efforts will be further supported by expertise from the Operations Management 
Team, the M&E Technical Working Group and the UNDAF 2012-2015
40
Technical Working Groups (TWGs)
Five UNDAF TWGs composed of UN agencies and 
implementing partners will work on key UNDAF pillars: 1) sustainable economic growth and risk reduction; 2) basic social services; 3) governance and capacity development; 4) women, youth and children; 
and 5) cross cutting issues. These five TWGs will be 
supported by expertise from three working groups: 
the Operations Management Team (OMT), the 
M&E Working Group; and the UN Communications 
Group. 
The main mechanism for the management and implementation of the M&E component of the UNDAF 
will be with the M&E Working Group, who will

Strengthening accountability and demonstrating results
Monitoring and evaluation are integral 
parts of the UNDAF and will follow the 
standard requirements and procedures as 
set out in the United Nations Development Group 
(UNDG) guidelines. To this end, an UNDAF M&E 
plan has been developed to ensure accountability, transparency and monitoring of progress and 
achievements of results against UNDAF outcomes 
and related outputs. The UNDAF M&E plan also 
includes activities aimed at capacity building of 
national partners to monitor progress towards the 
MDGs and GTP development goals, harmonize 
data collection systems and support database and 
analysis tools, as well as improve dissemination of 
findings. 
The objectively verifiable performance and coverage 
indicators formulated in the UNDAF results matrix 
will be used to measure progress at the outcomes 
level. An additional set of internationally recognized 
and standardized indicators has been proposed to assess the UN’s overall strategic intent, where possible, 
and to maximize national efforts to monitor major 
international commitments such as those reflected in 
the UNGASS, MDGs as well as the national GTP development goals.
The UNDAF will utilize Government information 
management systems and databases to monitor 
UNDAF indicators for which data are available.*
The Government undertakes surveys in areas such as 
EDHS, WMS, household income, consumption and 
expenditure, and a participatory poverty assessment.
